Originally from Scotland , but well established in Irish traditional music. Recorded by Mary Bergin, and Anne Conroy has a particularly fine version on a recording she made with Dublin singer Geraldine MacGowan which featured most of the band

Reedy Johnson’s

This is the Gmajor Reedy Johnson’s, the Dmajor one is more commonly known as ’Tom Steele’s“ or ”Hand Me Down the Tackle" This one is a very fun little single reel, that’s not too tricky for any player to master.

↳ Posted by b.maloney on January 22nd, 2007.

Miss Johnson’s would be the more common name, certainly
not Hand me down the tackle which is a completely different tune altogether

and it’s already at :
https://thesession.org/tunes/2411#sheetmusic

↳ Posted by Peter Laban on January 22nd, 2007.

Sorry for the confusion, this is the tune in G major known as Reedy Johnson’s, there is another in D major which is sometimes called “Hand me down the Tackle” as well as “Reedy Johnson’s”

Miss Johnson, X:8

This is the setting of this tune that is in Francis O’Neill’s 1001 tunes collection. Quite interesting, it has some differences from the way this tune is played nowadays. The biggest difference is the different order of the parts. But there are slight differences in the melody as well.

Kyle Borley play plays a very nice version of this tune, he published it in his YouTube Channel a few days back:

https://youtu.be/hbHDfCRV9Ds

↳ Posted by Fernando Durbán Galnares on May 21st, 2022.

Re: Miss Johnson

This is another tune title listed among the tunes named in the works of the County Wexford folklorist Patrick Kennedy, who names many tunes played by fiddlers and pipers in North West County Wexford in the early 1800’s. Miss Johnson is still a popular tune round these parts. (X7 is very close to the version usually played).

↳ Posted by John E Roche on October 17th, 2022.

Miss Johnson, X:12

Seamus Ennis version in The Pure Drop (played after the Leitrim Thrush).

As mentionned in a comment above, the Parts A and B are played in the reverse order than the others versions given here.

I keep the reverse order because that’s the way Seamus Ennis played this tune, and because it gives the tune a nice feel starting with the upper ocatve spectrum, and I like this a lot.

Playing in that order at the end of the set gives a kind of relief and peace.

↳ Posted by UPipes & harp on April 11th, 2024.
